_comment: Per-phase execution policy. 'kind' is the important field: 'code' phases are plain TypeScript in the conductor and never spawn a model — that is WHY no hook is needed to stop a model merging (docs/HOOKS.md §1). 'session' phases get one fresh Agent SDK query() that is never resumed.
_comment_cwd: 'worktree' = the leased git worktree for this ticket. 'conductor' = the Oneshot repo root, used by phases that must not see repo files at all.
_comment_writes: Filesystem scopes handed to hooks/write-scope.js via ONESHOT_WRITE_SCOPES. Anything outside is denied. 'run' expands to state/runs/<iid>/, 'artifacts' to state/runs/<iid>/artifacts/, 'memory' to state/memory/.

phases.name: recall
phases._why_skills: This phase was the last one whose whole method lived in a prompt string, and the method it held was the scoring ladder — file-path overlap, then module, then label, then title token — stated once, in four lines, with no room for what makes each rung worth its place. prior-art-recall carries it properly: that the ladder is ORDERED rather than summed (one shared file beats a label-plus-title match), that a title match alone is never enough because ERP titles repeat the same nouns across unrelated modules, that a card is read for its gotcha and its what-NOT-to-reuse rather than its summary (a later phase can re-derive what changed from the diff and can never re-derive what the last run abandoned), and that the brief is pasted VERBATIM into research, plan and implement, so its length is paid three times. It also states the one thing nothing else did: the index and the card store can disagree — this machine's memory has more cards under tickets/ than lines in index.jsonl — and the phase handles both directions without exploring. The prompt keeps the full short form, so a session that cannot resolve the skill still runs correctly; that is the same split reproductionBlock uses for bug-reproduction.

phases.name: research
phases._why_budget: Raised from 120 turns / 45m when research began reproducing reported bugs in the real app: bring-up of a warm app is seconds but a cold one is ~2m, the login is a handful of turns, and driving the steps costs ~12 turns per step-set, as it does for verify.
phases._why_skills: Reproduction is the `Bug` label's job, the same way `frontend-accessibility` is the `Accessibility` label's at plan — see that phase's `_why_skills`. It was an every-ticket skill until an accessibility ticket carrying no Bug label spent 57 turns and 528k weighted tokens failing to bring the app up for a verdict of 'inconclusive': asking a session to decide bug-vs-feature from the ticket's prose costs the app bring-up whether or not the answer is yes, and triage already knows. An absent label is the answer, not a missing signal. Moving this line back into `skills` restores the old behaviour, prose included — src/phases/prompts.ts gates the instructions on this same resolved list. `skills` is no longer empty: prior-art-survey rides along with the trace on EVERY ticket, because the survey is not a second job but a use for files this phase has already paid to open. It moved here from plan, which had 50 turns and the whole reuse hunt while this phase has 180 and the code already in front of it. The measurement that moved it: across seven dry replays of one ticket, a plan sent to DISCOVER the helper found it once in two attempts and spent 39 turns doing it, while the same helper handed over in `codePath` was used twice out of two, at 17 turns and for less money. Searching was never the failure — every run ran the right search; resolving a hit to the function containing it is what lapsed, which is why the skill makes that a command rather than a habit. The skill also carries the part no prompt had room for: that a name search finds a callable and misses the mirror, the duplicate and the unnamed fragment entirely. What the survey costs THIS phase is not measured: `--from research` does not run under DRY_RUN, so those replays measured plan only. The baseline is the six most recent runs before it whose run.json records research `ok` — 8768, 8770, 8774, 8778, 8782 and 8783, eight sessions because two of them ran research twice in lap 0: 27–80 turns and $1.57–5.91 a session, median 44 turns, each read from that session's `success` result in transcripts/research-lap0.jsonl. Count by run.json, not by a transcript's last line: three of those six end on a 0-turn error written after the success, and a run whose research `failed` is not a baseline. #63 adds 46 turns / $2.33 on one more ticket. Two of the eight sessions already passed 60, so one long session is not the signal: if the MEDIAN session climbs past ~60 turns, or any session reaches the 70% landing line (126 of 180), narrow the survey or gate it on a label; #63 is the issue that owns that measurement.

phases.name: design
phases._why: The Design label asks for the UI to be AGREED before it is built, so this sits between research (which has just traced where the UI lives) and plan (which would otherwise decide the shape itself). It produces mockups and screenshots; the conductor posts them to the ticket and the design gate parks the run until a dev approves. HEAVY because the job is making a mockup read as OUR app with the feature in it rather than a generic dashboard, which is exactly the judgement a cheaper model does badly — it reaches for a plausible-looking default. onFail 'retry' with one retry, then block. abort would match research and plan, but those abort on budgets we have MEASURED and this one is an estimate — a session hitting an unmeasured cap and killing the run is a worse trade than retrying once and stopping for a person. Revisit once real runs have corrected the number. Either way a Design ticket never reaches plan without a design, which is what the label exists to guarantee.
phases._why_n: 1.5, not 2, and the fraction is load-bearing. `n` is read in exactly one place — the numeric sort in config.ts — but phase NUMBERS are quoted in fifteen model-facing prompt headings ('## Plan (phase 2) — this is your specification'). Renumbering to insert an integer here would rewrite every one of those strings, and they are read by models as ground truth. A fraction sorts correctly and leaves them all true.
phases._why_cwd_port: cwd 'worktree' because the tokens have to come from the real frontend (Theme.js, style.js, _variables.scss) rather than from taste, and research.json is read from the run. needsPort because the phase screenshots the CURRENT screens off the running base branch: that is the 'before' half of every pair, and it is also how a mockup inherits the real shell instead of inventing one. It costs no wall clock — the app is already warming from the worktree lease — the flag only makes an empty pool fail here rather than halfway through.
phases._why_writes: 'artifacts', NOT 'worktree'. Mockup HTML committed to the ticket branch would land in the MR diff, and six HTML files inside a 200-line review is a worse review. Keeping them in state/runs/<iid>/artifacts/design/ also means a second design round after feedback does not dirty the branch.
phases._why_turns: 115 is an ESTIMATE, not a measurement — the first real runs should correct it, the way verify went 200->300->450 and research 60->120. Derived from verify's measured ~12 turns per browser interaction: ~15 to capture the current screens, ~10 for tokens, ~8 per mockup across ~5 screens, plus headroom. The prototype (~25) and the walkthrough recording (~20) are deliberately NOT in this number: they are the most expensive and most breakable part of the guess, so they follow in their own change once a few real runs have said what the base number actually is.

phases.name: plan
phases._why_layer_skills: Backend/Frontend are set at grooming by Jev (backend 93%, frontend 88%, 0 wrong skips on 42 tickets). Plan gets that layer's standards. At implement the labels only add an agent to the plan's forecast; where there is no plan, or it names no layer, the labels decide instead of listing both (labelledLayers in src/phases/prompts.ts).
phases._why_skills: `skills` is this phase's method, loaded for every ticket. `labelSkills` is the domain knowledge a particular ticket calls for, keyed by the label triage puts on it — reuse and approach are decided here, so an accessibility ticket needs that standard at plan time and not first at implement. One line adds the next pair; nothing in code changes. change-scoping replaces the vendored pair (planning-methodology, util-reuse-methodology) because the discovery half of their method now runs in research, where the files are already open: this phase CONFIRMS what arrived in `codePath` and searches only the residual its own approach introduces, which the vendored skills could not describe because they were written for a phase that was handed nothing. Neither vendored file is edited or deleted — util-reuse-agent still loads util-reuse-methodology under erp-code-review, and src/lib/claudedir.ts is explicit that Oneshot fills gaps and never shadows the context repo. This is a reclaim at a different moment in the pipeline, discovery-time versus review-time, not a move.
phases._why_django_scheduled_jobs: The only domain skill declared at plan, here because the mechanism it governs is chosen at plan time and is expensive to revisit later. ERP #8344 is the case: the plan proposed seeding `PeriodicTask`/`CrontabSchedule` rows in a data migration for a recurring reminder, citing `apps/costing/utils.py` as precedent — which is a per-entity one-off task, a different shape. Nothing the phase read said otherwise, so the wrong mechanism entered the plan and every later phase inherited it as a settled question. Scheduling is the rare case `implement` cannot recover: by then the migration is written, and `review` checks the diff against the plan rather than the plan against the repo. Deliberately NOT in `labelSkills`, which would be the tidier home — that needs triage to already know it is a scheduling ticket, and not knowing is the entire failure. 6KB against change-scoping's ~12KB, affordable only because the skill was split out of `django-management-commands`; the command-writing half stays at implement, reached through `django-backend-standards`.
phases._why_superpowers_planning: change-scoping decides WHAT this change touches and WHERE each unit goes; it says nothing about how a step is WRITTEN. That gap is what `implement` paid for -- a transcript audit of 46 implement laps measured 8.2 reads per edit, much of it re-deriving the signatures and call shapes a step had named only in prose. This vendors the superpowers writing-plans discipline, adapted for an autonomous phase (no interactive approval gate -- the pipeline's own plan/design/testcase gates stand in for it): each step is right-sized to one independently verifiable deliverable, its `what` names the exact symbols, signatures and values it adds or changes (never 'add validation' or 'handle edge cases'), its `files` lists every path it touches, and the set is self-reviewed for acceptance-criteria coverage and for name consistency across steps. A step written that way is exactly what lets `implement` and its sub-agents open a file to EDIT it rather than re-trace it, so this pairs with the trust-the-trace change at implement. ADDITIVE to change-scoping, not a replacement: scoping routes findings into reuse/risks/openQuestions/outOfScope, this shapes steps[] and nothing invents a schema field the plan does not already have.
phases._why_turns: 115 / 40m, raised from 50 / 20m. The prior budget was held low on seven dry replays of one ticket (26, 34, 31, 39, 34, 17, 35 turns — a maximum of 39 against 50), with one explicit condition for revisiting: a measurement showing a confirm-and-residual plan hitting the cap. #8933 is that measurement. It is a greenfield sub-module (Training Analytics) whose new table, KPI, bar-chart and person-picker idioms research cannot pre-trace because the components do not exist yet, so plan legitimately re-opened the frontend to place and reuse them; its lap0 failed error_max_turns at 50/50, overran the context window, and wrote no plan.json, and remediate cleared it only for the block to return. The replays measured CONTAINED changes to an existing surface; a new feature of this size is a different envelope and 50 turns does not hold it. 115 / 40m matches design, the heavy-tier sibling with comparable read-and-write load. The earlier caution still stands — a ceiling is read as a target — so the signal to act on next is a measurement showing contained plans drifting toward 115, and the answer then is to split the budget by ticket size, not to raise it again.
phases._why_beta: Beta is mapped on every phase that plans, builds, checks or shows the change, because it changes how the change SHIPS rather than what one phase knows: plan lays out v1, v2 and the switch, implement builds them, testcases writes the switch and v1-regression cases that verify then executes and nothing else does, base-check re-runs any of those verify marks 'pre-existing' against the base where v1 is all that exists, review holds the diff against v1's files, ui-evidence shows both versions, and mr tells the MR reviewer what retiring v1 takes. base-check is on demand and the rest run in order; dropping the label from any of them breaks the chain there — a switch no case covers is a switch nobody verified, a v1-regression the base-check cannot place is a regression that keeps its pass. The instructions are gated on this same resolved list in src/phases/prompts.ts (betaRequested), so removing the line from a phase removes the skill and its prose there together.
phases._why_ponytail: Declared here as well as at implement, because ponytail's first rungs — does this need to exist, is it already in this codebase — are approach decisions, and this is the phase that makes them. At implement the skill sits behind the lazy SKILL_LINE ('invoke the ones your change actually touches'), so the session decides from the plan whether a cross-cutting skill applies, and mostly it decides no: of the ten implement lap-0 sessions since ponytail was added (226, 8652, 8764, 8768, 8782, 8783, 8799, 8800, 8877, 8878) three invoked it — 226, 8782 and 8878. Here it was never offered: 0 of the 54 plan transcripts under state/runs invoke it, and the 25 since run 260 list it only in the init message's available skills. Plan's SKILL_LINE is eager, so this runs on every ticket, and the plan it shapes is the spec implement is told to follow. Unmeasured: whether plans get smaller. ~3KB against change-scoping's ~12KB; if plan's turn budget tightens, this is the cheapest skill to withdraw. On a Beta ticket the plan's beta duty carries the same carve-out implement's does, so rung 2 does not fold v2's copies back into v1.

phases.name: implement
phases._why_turns: 220 / 90m is the budget this phase was BORN with and, unlike research (60->120->180) and verify (200->300->450), it was never measured until a transcript audit of 46 captured implement laps: median ~$3.46 a lap at lap 0, ~$0.97 on a cycle lap, and the cap is the binding constraint on exactly ONE of the 46 (a lap-0 session: 220 turns, $17.60). So 220 is KEPT -- the cost is per-lap burn, not the ceiling. The burn is exploration: ~65% of tool calls were reads, 8.2 reads per edit overall, split 53/47 between the parent session and the sub-agents it dispatches, both re-opening files research's codePath already traced; cycle laps ran 15 reads per edit for a median of 4 edits. The levers that followed targeted the re-exploration directly -- the implement prompt's trust-the-trace block (src/phases/prompts.ts) and the conditional reuse sweep in context/agents/backend-agent.md and frontend-agent.md -- NOT this number. Revisit the cap only with a measurement showing a trust-the-trace lap reaching it; the single lap that already did was a reuse-hunt this change removes.
phases._why_skills: ponytail plus the layer standards and the two lint/migration gates. The skill files themselves are UNCHANGED, and two of them still order a search before writing: ponytail's rung 2 ('already in this codebase?') and react-frontend-standards' shared-component search. What changed is precedence, stated where these skills are loaded rather than inside each one: the implement prompt (src/phases/prompts.ts) tells the session, and context/agents/backend-agent.md and frontend-agent.md tell the sub-agents, that a handed trace replaces a skill's search for the surfaces it names, while a surface no phase surveyed still gets it. The trace counts only where a survey happened -- a kind-prefixed codePath entry or a verdict in plan's reuse; codePath can arrive empty or bare, and then the prompt says so and the full search applies. Plan's steps are part of what implement executes as written: plan loads superpowers-planning, which writes each step naming its symbols, signatures and files for an executor with no context, and implement forwards a step to its sub-agent verbatim. The audit above is why: 73 reuse greps and 21 Explore-agent dispatches across the laps were re-running phases 0-2's job.

phases.name: mr-open
phases._why: Opens the MR the moment `implement` has produced code, so every gate that follows has a readable diff. The test-case gate asks a person to approve scenarios at phase 4; before this existed the MR was not opened until phase 8, so that person was asked to approve test cases for a change they could not see. Code, not a session: pushing a branch and posting an MR is deterministic, and paying a model for it would add tokens, latency and a way to get it wrong. DRAFT, because nothing here has been reviewed, verified or evidenced yet -- `mr` takes the marker off once it has written the real description, which is also what stops `merge` meeting a draft it cannot merge. onFail is warn on purpose: an early MR is a convenience for the humans reading the gates, `mr` still opens one at phase 8 if this could not, and a run must not die because a courtesy push failed. SCOPED to the erp target. The MR-before-the-gates ordering was asked for while moving to that project, and an ungated phase would have changed the pipeline for every conductor on every project the moment it pulled -- including leaving a draft MR behind on runs that abort between here and `mr`, which those runs did not do before. It runs only when GITLAB_REPO_URL names a project called erp; for any other project, or with the URL unset, this phase does not exist and the sequence is exactly what it was. ONESHOT_PROJECT no longer selects anything, so unsetting it does not switch this off.

phases.name: testcases
phases._why_skills: The phase authors the list a QA reviewer signs off on and the list `verify` later executes, and until now it was the only session phase declaring no method at all — it wrote cases from the prompt alone while `plan` had a declared method (change-scoping, planning-methodology before it) and `verify` had local-browser-verify. erp-ticket-test-plan is where the scenario taxonomy (happy / negative / edge / boundary / side-effects) and the expected-value-from-business-logic rule live, so declaring it makes the authored list answerable to the same standard a person would apply. It is also where the feedback-intent routing lives — the rule that a correction edits a case in place instead of being appended as a new one. That rule had no reader on this path: the skill was reachable in the worktree but nothing required it, so the phase never consulted it.
phases._why: Opus, and its own phase: the list is written once, reviewed as a list, and executed by verify against a real browser — which is what makes 'the change passes its own cases' a claim about something a person could re-run rather than about whatever the verifying session happened to think of. It runs AFTER implement so the cases can name the real symbols and routes the change actually produced — the cost of that is a list authored with the implementation in view, so the prompt makes the acceptance criteria, not the diff, the source of truth.
phases._why_turns: 40 was never sized for this job — it is the number this phase was born with in 37f3978, when testcases was n:3 and ran BEFORE implement, authoring from the ticket and the plan with nothing to read. 0d64e2d moved the block to n:4 verbatim while the prompt gained implement's artifact, 'read git diff before you start' and 'read whatever you need to'. The job doubled; the budget did not move, and unlike verify (200->300->450) and research (60->120) it never got a measured raise. Run 237 (r-mtvacbt9-7a23b5) is where that came due: 40 turns spent entirely on context-gathering, 11,719 output tokens, not one case written, and onFail abort blocked the run. The driver is NOT diff size — that diff was 9 files and 211 insertions. It is whether the diff carries the UI vocabulary the cases need: run 8 changed loginTestIds.js and displayText.js and finished in 26 turns, run 19 was backend-only and finished in 18, and run 237 was a date-math fix behind a browser modal, so the routes, the permission gate and the PL_* labels all had to be excavated from files the diff never touched. research.uiPath now supplies that vocabulary, which is what makes 110 a real ceiling rather than a bigger number in front of an unbounded search. 30 minutes because the 15 was equally inherited, and this phase has already died on the CLOCK once (r-mtfu7ph1-e56363, 119 stream messages, no result).

phases.name: review
phases._why_group: testcases and review both consume only implement's output and neither reads the other's artifact, so they run concurrently. The one interaction — a review cycle lap re-entering implement — leaves testcases pinned (the case list is written once), so the group simply degrades to review alone on later laps. A pending test-case approval gate (src/conductor/reviewgate.ts) is a second exception: the runner holds review back out of the batch so the gate gets a solo iteration to check it, rather than the two running concurrently and the gate never firing.

phases.name: testcases-eval
phases._why: ON DEMAND: the conductor invokes it inside the testcases slot, once per evaluation of a freshly written list, and never after the Review gate asks for a revision. It judges the list against the TICKET — requirements frozen on the first attempt, coverage mapped onto them after — and the conductor (src/lib/testcaseseval.ts) decides from its findings whether testcases re-runs: at most twice, and no further once a re-run closes no gap. Read-only (writes: []) because it reads the diff for evidence and changes nothing. Standard tier: it judges a list, it does not write one.
phases._why_n: 5.5, not 4.5: phases() sorts by n, and anything between testcases (4) and review (5) would split the check group the runner batches. Being on demand it never runs in its sorted slot; n only decides where it sits in the list.

phases.name: verify
phases._why_turns: Measured live: driving webpack + the real login form through Bash-run Playwright costs ~12 turns per case, so the cap must scale with the list. A 20-case list (run #6) exhausted a 200-turn cap at case 17 and was salvaged from partial — an incomplete verdict that still gates the merge. 300 turns / 120 min fits a 20-case list with headroom; a verify that dies at max_turns produces a partial artifact, and the cycle it triggers re-pays implement and review for what was only a budget problem.
phases._why_skills: local-browser-verify is how the app comes up and how a case is driven; erp-ticket-test-data is how the state a case asserts against is MADE. Only the first was declared, so the phase had a method for the browser and none for the database — and it improvised one per session. The case rests on structure, not on any one incident: verify drives a real app against ONE local Postgres that every worktree shares (hrdb/local_settings.py is copied unchanged into each, and up to three app ports can be live at once), so whatever a session writes outlives it and can collide with a concurrent run. The verify.json artifacts show the shape, described here by behaviour because run iids live in each machine's own ledger and do not resolve on another: a drag case's persisted move left a later case unable to reach the empty column it needed; several cases blocked together on pre-existing incomplete day-log rows that a session tried to hand-fix and ran out of budget on; a case was skipped because the combination of rows it needed was not fabricated within the turn budget. Discovery-first, transaction rollback for a measurement, idempotent get_or_create and marker-plus-cleanup tracking answer exactly those, and they are already written down in that skill. It is shaped for a person on dev/stage with a webshell, which this phase is not — src/phases/prompts.ts carries the boundaries that reframe it (the one shared local DB via the venv shell, committed-and-marked data for anything the browser must see, and no user to hand a script to), the same way research's prose and its skill are gated together.

phases.name: base-check
phases._why_beta: base-check runs the cases verify marked 'pre-existing' against a second app on the base branch, and the base branch is v1 only — no v2, no switch, no stored choice. Without the label the session reaches for the switch a case's steps name and cannot find it, and judges scope from the ticket text, which the Beta label never reaches. The duty tells it both: run v1's flow directly on the base, and treat every v1-regression, switch or v2 case as this ticket's own scope so a v1-regression that fails goes back to being a fail instead of keeping the label. On demand, so it is reached only when verify hands it a 'pre-existing' case.
phases._why: ON DEMAND: the conductor invokes it only when verify marks a case 'pre-existing'. That label neither cycles to implement nor blocks the merge, so it is a claim with teeth, and a check phase's claim about itself is not evidence. This phase re-runs ONLY those cases against a second app on the base branch; the conductor keeps the label for a case that fails there too and that the session judged outside this ticket's scope, and turns every other one back into a fail (applyBaseCheck in src/conductor/runner.ts). Scope is judged here, from the ticket and its criteria, because a case covering the ticket's own change fails on the base by definition; a 'happy'-tagged case never reaches this phase at all. Neither does a branch that adds or changes a migration: every app shares one Postgres that verify already migrated forward, so a base app there runs base code on the branch's schema and is no second opinion (sharedDatabaseRefusal). Unproven is not proven: a base app that will not come up, or a session that answers nothing, confirms nothing, and the cases count as failures exactly as they did before the label existed. A session that DIES is not an answer either, and never spends a verify lap on a check nobody ran (baseCheckOutcome). A cancel, a pause, a usage limit or an account gate is not re-attempted: verify is recorded infra and the existing stop, park and gate paths decide. A pause counts as a death whatever the session returned, because pause-check.cjs makes a session stop and summarize rather than killing it. Only a plain infra death (a timeout, a stall, a killed spawn) is re-attempted in place, and past that the run blocks instead of re-running verify, because every verify re-run would start those re-attempts over. writes run+artifacts and NOT worktree: the base app is brought up in its own checkout the way ui-evidence takes its 'before' shots, and this session must never be able to edit the branch whose verdict it is checking. onFail warn because the conductor already reads a failed check as unconfirmed. 120 turns / 40 min is an ESTIMATE for 1-3 cases at verify's measured ~12 turns per case plus a base bring-up; correct it from real runs.

phases.name: mr
phases._why_group: ui-evidence drives the browser on the leased port while mr pushes the branch and writes the MR — disjoint tools, disjoint writes, both read-only on the diff. Running them together hides the screenshot pass inside the MR pass's wall clock.

phases.name: demo-recording
phases._why: Records a short annotated walkthrough of the merged-ready feature working in the real app and posts the webm to the ticket, so a stakeholder sees the change move without checking out the branch. It sits AFTER `ui-evidence` (7) and `mr` (8) and before `merge` (9): the feature is implemented, verified, evidenced and the MR carries its real description, so the journey the demo drives is the one that actually passed, not a draft `mr-open` left of an unverified branch. SESSION, not code: the walkthrough is ticket-specific judgement — which single user journey tells the story, sourced from the acceptance criteria and verify's happy-path cases — and only a model can author that from the ticket. needsPort because it drives the leased app through Playwright, cwd 'worktree' so it reads this run's verify.json / testcases.json and the real routes, writes 'run'+'artifacts' (the webm and demo.json land in state/runs/<iid>/artifacts/, never on the branch, the same reason `design` and `ui-evidence` keep their media out of the diff). The webm reaches the ticket the way every other artefact reaches GitLab here: the conductor publishes it from demo.json (src/lib/publish.ts, the `demo` spec beside `ui-evidence`), because session phases are off every GitLab write tool (toolPolicy in src/conductor/phase.ts) — the session records and names the webm, it does not post. This is a DIFFERENT artefact from `ui-evidence`, and the one rule they invert: evidence forbids any DOM overlay because a screenshot must be the untouched app, while a demo REQUIRES caption chrome — the overlay is narration, drawn to read as demo furniture and never as the app's own UI; the skill owns that line.
phases._why_gating: labelGated 'Demo', and no `targets` — exactly `design`'s shape ('Design', untargeted). It is OPT-IN: a human tags the ticket, so it never fires on a backend-only change where a browser walkthrough shows nothing, and it changes no conductor's pipeline SHAPE on pull, because a labelGated phase only runs where the label is carried. That is the difference from `mr-open`, the one phase that IS target-scoped: mr-open reorders the MR against the gates for everyone on the project the moment they pull, so it had to be fenced to erp (phase-targets.test.ts guards that it is the only one). This phase reorders nothing and appears only when someone asks for it, so a target gate would buy nothing and would weaken that canary.
phases._why_fail: onFail 'warn', not 'retry'. A demo is a courtesy artefact: a capture that fails must never block a change that is already verified, reviewed and evidenced from merging — the same call `ui-evidence` and `mr-open` make. The single re-run the recording deserves lives INSIDE the session (the skill attempts the walkthrough once, retries the capture once on a flaky step or a failed upload), because the runner's `onFail: retry` BLOCKS once its retries are spent (afterFailure in src/conductor/runner.ts), which is exactly the block this phase must not produce. On a final failure the session posts a short note to the ticket with the reason there is no demo, so the gap is recorded where a person will see it rather than swallowed; a hard session death still degrades to 'warned' and the run proceeds to merge.
phases._why_turns: 90 / 40m is an ESTIMATE, correct it from real runs. Shaped from `ui-evidence` (80/40, the nearest phase: one leased app, Playwright, a GitLab upload) plus headroom for the single in-session re-run and the one video encode. The app is already warm from the lease, so bring-up is reuse-cheap; the cost is driving one journey of ~5-8 steps, not verify's whole case list, which is why it is well under verify's cap.

phases.name: merge
phases._why: Code, not a session, and now the LAST phase. No model holds a merge tool, so v1's label-guard approval check has nothing to guard — and with deploy, qa, demo, memorize and document removed, the pipeline's definition of done is 'merged into the base branch'. The success notes this phase posts to the ticket and the MR are therefore the run's only durable record besides the MR itself; the exit label swap still happens in finish(), which is where every terminal status has always been decided.

phases.name: remediate
phases._why: ON DEMAND, and that field is the design: the main loop never schedules this phase, the conductor invokes it when another phase blocks. It exists because nearly every block this pipeline has produced was ENVIRONMENTAL and not a defect — a credential the demo snapshot does not carry, an account missing the group a feature is gated behind, a wedged MCP spawn that left a session with no tools at all, a turn cap that fitted the work when it was written. Those are diagnosable without a person, and the alternative is a watcher logging 'blocked cooldown' once a minute until someone runs an unblock command by hand. HEAVY tier because this is diagnosis from indirect evidence — a turn count, an absent artifact, a reason line — which is precisely the job a cheaper model does badly: it pattern-matches to the last failure it saw. cwd 'conductor' because the cause is almost never inside the ticket's worktree, and a phase that cannot see the diff cannot be tempted to fix it. writes 'run' only, so its repairs are ACTIONS on the environment rather than edits to this repo; config/ and src/ are denied to every phase by the write-scope hook in any case, which is why a too-small turn cap comes back as humanNeeded rather than as a patch. onFail 'warn' because a remediation that fails leaves the run exactly as blocked as it already was — making that an abort would give the recovery path teeth the thing it recovers from does not have.

phases.name: mr-feedback
phases._why_skills: The dispositions' definitions and the output contract are owned by the prompt (src/mrfeedback/prompts.ts triagePrompt); the skill's table only restates them. What the skill adds is the JUDGEMENT the prompt does not carry — what clears the bar for `decline`, why a merely inconvenient request is a `fix`, how small a `plan` has to stay, and the fact that a reply cannot @mention anyone because respond.ts neutralises it. That is skill-shaped, and it was prose nobody could edit without touching TypeScript.
phases._why: ON DEMAND: the merge phase finds new review threads on the run's MR and the runner invokes this to decide what each one needs — fix, already-done, question or decline. HEAVY because declining a reviewer or answering a question from the code is judgement, and a wrong 'fix' costs a full implement→verify lap. cwd 'worktree' so it reads the actual diff; writes 'run' only and no GitLab write tools (phase.ts), so it can neither change the code nor post — the conductor replies after the fixes are verified. onFail 'blocked' because an untriaged comment is a reviewer nobody answered; infra deaths still retry for free, since re-entering merge re-detects the same threads. See src/mrfeedback and config/mr-feedback.json.

phases.name: local-tests-scope
phases._why: The local automation tests mode's one session (src/localtests). ON DEMAND: the Loop never schedules it, and the mode invokes it by name (runPhase) for a ticket carrying labels.localTestsTrigger — which the Loop puts on beside labels.exit when it merges the ticket — whose merge request is MERGED into branches.base. Its 'worktree' is a throwaway ERP checkout of that MR's merge commit, so the change it reads is the merge commit against its first parent. It decides which workstream-automation (Cypress) specs run — the ones the change reaches, up to 3 that go through the screen it changed (from the analysis's screenSpecs), and the main-functionality (smoke) specs of every module the change touched — and prepares them, so QA approves an exact list (the impacted-module report on the ticket) and the run executes exactly that list. A session because one part of it is a judgement a script cannot make: whether a renamed testid was MEANT (follow it with a temporary edit of the existing spec) or is a regression (leave the spec to fail), and which specs cannot run on a desk. The counting and the main-functionality picks are not a judgement, so they are not left to the session: skills/local-tests-impact/scripts/index.cjs maps the diff, picks each module's mainSpecs, counts the cases and prices the list, and the code adds back any main spec the session left out without a reason. It never writes or suggests a test: a new spec file in its worktree is refused, and only tests that exist in workstream-automation run.
phases._why_n: 13, after every phase the Loop runs, although the mode it belongs to runs after the merge anyway. A phase between ui-evidence and mr, even an on-demand one the Loop steps over, would split their 'package' group, because a group is a run of CONSECUTIVE phases. At the end of the list it changes nothing the Loop does.
phases._why_writes: 'run' and nothing wider, and it is enough: the throwaway automation worktree the conductor checks out before this session (prepare-scope) is state/runs/<iid>/wsa, inside the run directory, so the session can edit specs, page objects and fixtures there and cannot touch the ERP worktree. git-guard keeps git from changing that repo at all, and the conductor saves the edits as artifacts/local-tests/temporary-changes.patch and removes the worktree the moment the session ends (capture), checking every changed file against localTests.allowedPaths.
phases._why_onFail: warn, and inert: the mode handles a scope that could not be made itself (it says so on the ticket and runs nothing) and never goes through the Loop's policy.
phases._why_budget: standard tier and 80 turns / 30 min, like ui-evidence, and an ESTIMATE: index.cjs answers in about a second, so the budget is for reading the diff, pricing one or two candidate lists and a handful of one-line selector edits. Correct it from real runs.
phases._why_targets: Scoped to the erp target, whose automation suite this is. On a desk where localTestsConfig() is off (no ONESHOT_LOCAL_TESTS_REPO, localTests.enabled false, or a local-tests label left empty) the mode never starts, so nothing invokes this phase there.

phases.name: local-tests-run
phases._why: Code, not a session, and not in the Loop's CODE_PHASES. ON DEMAND, so the Loop steps over it; the local automation tests mode (src/localtests) runs it once QA approves the list, through src/conductor/localtests.ts, which drives scripts/localtests.cjs against the MR's merge commit with the merge commit's first parent as the base. It is the LAST phase of a ticket: its results note — the automation report — is the last thing Oneshot posts, and it marks the ticket labels.localTestsDone, passed or failed. The entry stays because it is this run's configuration: its artifact and the timeoutMin below. Copying the baseline database, applying the scope's patch to a fresh automation worktree, running Cypress and reading its results is deterministic, and no model should hold the automation credentials or a database it could write to. Idempotent by cache key: the specs, the code under test, the automation commit and the patch. One Cypress run per desk (src/lib/cypresslease.ts): a busy desk PARKS the run rather than failing it, and the next tick tries again. Same target scope and desk switch as local-tests-scope, and placed after it at the end of the list for the reason its _why_n gives.
phases._why_onFail: warn, and inert like local-tests-scope's. A setup failure (no baseline database, a patch that no longer applies, a script that died) is the desk's problem: the ticket gets the reason and labels.localTestsTrigger back, so the run is tried again, and it is not marked done. Failing TESTS are not a failure of this step at all: they are posted with the rest of the results and the ticket is marked labels.localTestsDone.
phases._why_timeoutMin: The FLOOR of the conductor's own kill, and the one place this code phase reads its timeoutMin. The script holds each Cypress run to localTests.maxRunMinutes, but around that it copies the database, migrates, builds the ticket's app (25 minutes allowed cold) and, when tests failed, builds the base app and re-runs the failures to say whether they fail on dev too. So the conductor kills the script's whole process group at the LATER of maxRunMinutes + 15 and this: the first alone (60 minutes today) would cut exactly the runs that needed the most building, usually in the middle of the base re-run. 120 is an ESTIMATE of a cold build, a full Cypress run and a base re-run; correct it from real runs (runDeadlineMs in src/lib/cypresslease.ts).
